title: ChatGPT Goes to Law School
pub: Journal of Legal Education, vol. 71, no. 3 (Spring 2022, published 2023), pp. 387-400
author: Jonathan H. Choi · Kristin E. Hickman · Amy B. Monahan · Daniel Schwarcz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The study accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI has uneven, task-dependent capabilities and is best deployed as supervised augmentation rather than wholesale lawyer replacement. It materially extends the proposition with blind-graded evidence identifying specific strengths and failures in legal analysis, and with concrete implications for lawyer workflows, prompting and legal education.
qs: As a result, ChatGPT’s performance tended to be highly uneven, scoring near or even above the average on some questions, and near zero on other questions.

A lawyer could have ChatGPT prepare the initial draft of a memo and then tweak that draft as needed; she could use ChatGPT to draft her way out of writer’s block; she could use ChatGPT to produce an initial batch of arguments and then winnow them down to the most effective; she could use ChatGPT to adapt past examples of legal documents to make her work more efficient.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The source directly supports combining foundational legal research and reasoning with preparation for lawyer-led AI use. It also aligns with the cluster’s distinction between assessments of unaided competence and AI-assisted practice, recommending explicit rules and targeted technology restrictions rather than treating AI permission as a single all-or-nothing question.

Professors who want to test unassisted recall of legal rules and unassisted analysis should therefore establish guidelines for the use of these technologies in advance.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source supports the distinction between mere AI exposure and professional readiness. It advocates preparing students for AI-assisted practice while preserving independent legal research and reasoning, and it recommends explicit restrictions when assessing unaided competence. Its predictions about practical benefits remain qualified rather than evidence of durable capability.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious distinction between demonstrated task-specific capability and autonomous professional competence. Its blind-graded exam results show limited but real legal-task performance, while its recommendations preserve independent legal research and reasoning and favor preparation for supervised, effective use. It does not directly address access-to-justice outcomes, UPL boundaries or provider reform.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core account: ChatGPT showed limited but meaningful performance on bounded legal assessments, while its practical value lies in lawyer-supervised drafting and ideation rather than autonomous practice. It also reinforces the competence-risk theme by urging law schools to teach effective AI use while preserving students’ independent legal research and reasoning skills.

kp.k: Study tested standardized AI answers against actual student exams
kp.d: The authors tested the December 15, 2022 distribution of ChatGPT on ninety-five multiple-choice questions and twelve essay questions across Constitutional Law, Employee Benefits, Taxation and Torts at the University of Minnesota. Answers used standardized prompts rather than question-specific human adaptation. AI exams were mixed with student exams for blind grading, except Taxation, which was entirely multiple choice. AI results were removed before recalculating actual student grades. This tests largely unassisted exam production, not collaborative legal practice.
qs: In all cases, we generated answers using the December 15, 2022, distribution of ChatGPT.
The AI-generated exams were then shuffled with actual student exams and graded blindly by the other three co-authors.
The Taxation exam was an exception, because it was entirely multiple choice and therefore did not need to be graded blind.

kp.k: Passing grades coexisted with near-bottom class rankings
kp.d: ChatGPT averaged C+, earning B in Constitutional Law (thirty-sixth of forty), B- in Employee Benefits (eighteenth of nineteen), C- in Taxation (sixty-sixth of sixty-seven), and C- in Torts (seventy-fifth of seventy-five). Courses curved to approximately B+ at a highly selective institution. The authors say this performance would earn credit but trigger academic probation; their hypothetical graduation claim assumes constant performance and excludes other graduation requirements involving different skills.
qs: Overall, ChatGPT passed all four classes based on its final exam, averaging a C+ across all exams, an outcome that would earn credit toward the J.D. but place a student on academic probation.
Despite performing sufficiently well to theoretically earn a J.D. degree, ChatGPT generally scored at or near the bottom of each class.
assuming its work remained constant throughout law school (and ignoring other graduation requirements that involve different skills)

kp.k: Essay performance exceeded multiple-choice performance but varied sharply
kp.d: Average essay performance was the seventeenth percentile, equally weighted across questions and exams, versus the seventh percentile for multiple choice, equally weighted across exams. Some essays matched or exceeded student averages; others received exceptionally low scores, especially when requiring course-specific cases, theories or doctrines. These findings qualify any interpretation of passing grades as consistent legal analytical competence.
qs: Its average percentile performance on the essay questions (equally weighted across questions and exams) was the seventeenth percentile; its average performance on the multiple-choice questions (equally weighted across exams) was the seventh percentile.
On the other hand, when ChatGPT’s essay questions were incorrect, they were dramatically incorrect, often garnering the worst scores in the class.

kp.k: Mathematical questions exposed a specific performance weakness
kp.d: ChatGPT answered twenty-one of twenty-five Constitutional Law multiple-choice questions correctly (reported p = 0.000) and six of ten Torts questions (p = 0.020). On Taxation, it answered eight of twenty-nine mathematical questions correctly, not significantly above chance (p = 0.443), compared with sixteen of thirty-one nonmathematical questions (p = 0.001). The authors also observed better performance on relatively uniform legal rules than jurisdictionally variable doctrines.
qs: On the Taxation exam, ChatGPT answered only eight out of twenty-nine mathematical questions correctly, essentially no better than chance (p = 0.443).
It answered sixteen out of thirty- one nonmathematical questions correctly (including questions involving numbers but no mathematical reasoning), significantly better than chance (p = 0.001).

kp.k: Alternative prompting methods did not outperform simple prompts
kp.d: Simple multiple-choice prompts produced 51/95 correct answers, compared with 44/95 for chain-of-thought and 47/95 for rank-order prompts. Differences were not statistically significant (p = 0.138 and p = 0.257 respectively), using bootstrapping with 100,000 iterations. The authors did not replicate previously reported advantages, but explicitly acknowledge that their small sample cannot rule out such advantages. They suggest differences in task, model or multiple comparisons as possible explanations rather than established causes.
qs: Of the three methods, the simplest performed the best, although the difference compared with the other methods was not statistically significant (p = 0.138 compared with CoT, p = 0.257 compared with rank-order).
As a result, we failed to replicate past studies in which CoT and rank-order prompting produced superior results.

kp.k: Legal rule synthesis and polished drafting were relative strengths
kp.d: The authors found strong basic doctrinal exposition, organization, tone and composition, including technical employee-benefits material. ChatGPT explained ERISA preemption using statutory language and Supreme Court cases and exceeded the class average on a short-answer prohibited-transactions question. Its grammatically polished prose and orderly structure nevertheless did not establish strong issue identification or application of law.
qs: In writing essays, ChatGPT displayed a strong grasp of basic legal rules and had consistently solid organization and composition.
ChatGPT even outperformed the class average when working through a short-answer question involving ERISA’s highly technical prohibited transaction rules.
Stylistically, ChatGPT produced text with no grammatical errors or typos.

kp.k: Issue spotting and factual application remained major weaknesses
kp.d: ChatGPT identified only one of five issues on the Constitutional Law issue spotter, missed distinct negligence theories and an employer-size threshold, and sometimes discussed irrelevant causes of action. It frequently stated rules without analyzing hypothetical facts, occasionally misunderstood technical terms, and did not consistently use IRAC because the researchers did not request it. The authors speculate, rather than demonstrate, that RLHF contributed to excessive reluctance to choose between competing factual interpretations.
qs: ChatGPT often struggled to spot issues when given an open-ended prompt, a core skill on law school exams.
One of the biggest problems with ChatGPT’s essays was that they failed to go into sufficient detail when applying legal rules to the facts contained within exam hypotheticals.
Because we did not prompt it to do so, ChatGPT did not consistently employ an “Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion” (IRAC) or similar structure in its essays.

kp.k: General legal knowledge did not reliably match course scope
kp.d: Answers introduced procedural due process and takings issues outside the tested Constitutional Law course and failed to engage with requested law-and-economics concepts in Torts. Supplying case names also led ChatGPT to rely on a different case sharing a name and to discuss portions of cases not taught. The researchers did not test whether more specific citations or excerpts would solve those problems.
qs: ChatGPT sometimes departed from the material covered in the relevant courses, because the precise scope of each course would have been impossible to exactly specify in prompts.

However, when given a list of cases by name only for the Constitutional Law exam, ChatGPT relied heavily in its answer on a case that was not covered in the course but shared a name with one that was.
We did not investigate whether prompting with more specific citations or excerpts could address this issue.

kp.k: Citation reliability findings were narrow and explicitly qualified
kp.d: The authors report little fabrication in this study and suggest anti-fabrication instructions and supplied case lists as possible reasons. They found reliable real case names and descriptions, not Bluebook citations, under specific instructions. Only Constitutional Law required case references, and widely discussed constitutional cases may have helped. An apparent performance benefit from requesting references was an exploratory observation, not a confident finding.
qs: However, we found that ChatGPT could reliably generate real case names (but not Bluebook citations) and accurately describe the contents of these cases when specifically instructed not to fabricate citations.
Note that only the Constitutional Law exam required case references, and ChatGPT may work particularly well here because constitutional cases are widely discussed.
Although our sample size is too small for any confident pronouncements, ChatGPT seemed to perform better when the exam required references

kp.k: Human collaboration is predicted to outperform standalone generation
kp.d: The authors anticipate students and lawyers improving results through course-specific prompts, generation of shorter issue-focused passages, and human supplementation of drafts with legal analysis and issue identification. These are predictions beyond the standardized-prompt experiment. They also suggest future models, legal specialization and better prompting could improve exam performance.
qs: This type of collaboration between a human and ChatGPT would almost certainly produce better results than using ChatGPT alone.
Future models or improvements in prompt engineering could therefore help language models to produce better law school exam answers.

kp.k: AI creates assessment risks and opportunities for legal education
kp.d: The authors predict particular benefits for low-performing and time-constrained students through rapid drafts and rule synthesis. They warn hypothetically that unrestricted remote use could enable a student to earn a credential that does not reflect readiness to practice. Recommendations include advance use guidelines, revised honor codes, possible technology restrictions and more analysis-focused questions. They caution that models' relative strengths across question types may change.
qs: We expect that ChatGPT could substantially improve the performance of students on exams.
This is especially true for low-performing students and those who suffer under time constraints.
Administrations should consider how to reshape honor codes to regulate the use of language models in general.
They might also reconsider the types of questions they pose to students, focusing on those that require analysis rather than those that simply require recall of legal rules.

kp.k: Practice implications favor augmentation over replacing legal reasoning
kp.d: The authors predict lawyers will use language models for initial memoranda, overcoming writer's block, generating candidate arguments and adapting existing documents. These are prospective efficiency applications, not measured practice outcomes. They recommend teaching effective use while retaining fundamental research and reasoning skills; their account keeps lawyers responsible for understanding sources and developing analysis.
qs: Based on our results, we also expect that language models will become helpful tools for practicing lawyers.
While ChatGPT and similar tools might help a lawyer work more efficiently, they cannot (yet) replace the need for a lawyer to locate, understand, and reason from relevant sources of law.

kp.k: Prompt engineering may become a legal writing skill
kp.d: Based on initial experimentation, the authors recommend concise tone instructions placed at the end, word ranges rather than exact targets, explicit anti-fabrication instructions, and sequential drafting from an introduction and table of contents. They report that summarizing long fact patterns can address context-window constraints but reduces factual detail. These are experience-based guidelines, not established universal best practices or demonstrated professional productivity gains.
qs: As lawyers learn to use ChatGPT as part of their legal practice, prompt engineering could become an essential part of legal writing.
We induced ChatGPT to produce longer answers by asking for an introduction and table of contents, and then asking for each section sequentially.
Summarizing reduces the level of factual detail that ChatGPT provides but can be necessary with very long essays.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Choi, Hickman, Monahan and Schwarcz predict that language models will assist legal drafting and improve lawyers’ efficiency, rather than currently replace lawyers’ legal research and reasoning.
pts.d: The authors envisage lawyers using ChatGPT to prepare initial memoranda, overcome writer’s block, generate arguments for subsequent selection, and adapt existing legal documents. They predict that human–AI collaboration will outperform unaided ChatGPT and suggest that prompt engineering could become an essential legal-writing skill. In legal education, they expect substantial exam-performance benefits, particularly for weaker or time-constrained students, alongside risks that AI-assisted credentials may not reflect independent ability. They recommend advance rules on AI use and consideration of assessment changes. These are implications and predictions drawn from an exam study, not measured effects on practicing lawyers’ productivity or legal markets.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of four University of Minnesota law-school examinations and the authors’ prompt-development experience; professional-use predictions extrapolate from those findings.
pts.d: The authors tested the December 15, 2022 distribution of ChatGPT on 95 multiple-choice and 12 essay questions in Constitutional Law, Employee Benefits, Taxation and Torts. Essay-containing exams were mixed with student submissions and blindly graded; the entirely multiple-choice Taxation exam did not require blind grading. Uniform prompts were used without question-specific adaptation. ChatGPT passed all four courses at an average C+ but ranked near or at the bottom: 36/40, 18/19, 66/67 and 75/75, respectively. Average essay performance was at the seventeenth percentile and multiple-choice performance at the seventh. Observed strengths included rule statements, organization and prose; weaknesses included issue identification, application of law to facts, mathematical reasoning and uneven performance. Simple multiple-choice prompting outperformed the alternatives numerically, but differences were not statistically significant. Recommendations on tone, citations and essay structure rest on preliminary experimentation, not a professional-workplace trial. The authors observed little fabrication under their prompts but explicitly qualified citation-related findings by sample size and subject matter.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings describe a late-2022 model; future improvements and adoption are anticipated without a dated forecast, and the graduation and collaboration claims are conditional.
pts.d: The authors distinguish current uneven performance from expected future usefulness. The hypothetical J.D. outcome assumes consistent performance across law school and excludes graduation requirements involving other skills; the observed average would also place a student on academic probation. The credential-integrity risk is framed around remote exams without restrictions on ChatGPT. Expected gains from collaboration depend on course-specific prompts, targeted drafting, and human supplementation of analysis and issue identification. Future models and improved prompting may improve exam performance, but the authors do not predict which question types will remain most resistant. Current citation success is qualified: only Constitutional Law required case references, widely discussed cases may be unusually suitable, and reliable case names did not imply reliable Bluebook citations. Context-window limits can impede long legal tasks, while summarization sacrifices factual detail.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified affected groups are practicing lawyers, law students, professors and law-school administrations; the source does not quantify effects on clients, staffing or legal-market segments.
pts.d: Practicing lawyers may gain drafting assistance and efficiency while retaining responsibility for substantive legal research and reasoning. Students may use AI for rule recall, draft generation and exam completion, with potentially greater benefits for low-performing students and those constrained by time. Professors and administrators face assessment-integrity, honor-code and technology-policy questions. Law schools are encouraged to prepare students for effective professional use while maintaining foundational legal skills. The paper does not establish changes in lawyer employment, firm leverage, fees, client costs or access to justice.
